newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand to take steps to boost exports, firms wary.
newsitem.headline: Thailand to take steps to boost exports, firms wary.

text.p: Top Thai policy makers vowed on Sunday to take concrete measures to help companies boost sagging exports but business leaders gave only a cautious welcome.

At a government-business Exports Summit chaired by Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh in this resort town, the government promised to cut exporters' costs by speeding up tax rebates, cutting interest rates and reducing other infrastructural costs.
But several measures had no clear-cut timeframes attached to them.

The governmment would also waive an import quota system for raw materials used in making products for exports such as powdered milk, said Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee after the one-day summit ended.
"The spoonful of sugar the government promised to give makes bitter pills like the bearish economy much easier to swallow," said one leading industrialist who asked not to be named.
"But they can rest assured that their actions will be measured against their words. We will closely monitor whether the government does implement these plans," he said.
Sluggish exports have added to Thailand's economic woes with private economists seeing gross domestic product growth this year at a decade-low of about six percent.

Chokechai Aksaranand, president of the Federation of Thai Industries said there will be another meeting between authorities and the private sector in the next two months to assess government performance on outstanding issues.
The government must reform the bureacracy to make it more efficient and to boost export competitiveness, he added.
Thai exports fell 0.2 percent in 1996 against an increase of of 23.6 percent in 1995.
But despite a slow start this year, Chavalit said he was confident that export growth for 1997 will meet the target of 10 percent set by the Commerce ministry.
"The April figures showed some sign of recovery in exports. I believe that with the scheme we announced today, exports this year will meet the target," he told reporters.
"There are several potential products that we can develop and make Thailand a center for these industries, such as foods, automobiles and (auto) parts, computers and electronics," he said.
Earlier, exporters told policy makers at a meeting here that the biggest problem facing the country's hard-hit exports was none other than the Thai government itself.
They lashed out at authorities for their failure to cut high interest rates, red tape, to deal with corruption in the customs department and the absence of a focused export strategy.
Thai lending rates at 12.75-13.00 percent are among the highest in the region and aimed at atracting short term capital as well as defending the recently-embattled baht.

On interest rate cuts, Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, who was also at the summit, said that despite some constraints in the money market, he believed the Bank of Thailand would be able to relax monetary policy.
Thai Bankers Association president Olarn Chaiprawat said he expected the Bank of Thailand to "make an unequivocal statement" on Monday to bring the lending rate down.
Analysts said Thai exports were undergoing structural as well as cyclical problems which had resulted in current problems.
Production of higher-value products had yet to reach full capacity while output in the labour-intensive sector had been hit by tough competition from lower-cost foreign producers.
